steps: Unpack & fit the standoffs
Check the contents, then fit the top and rear standoffs. Fitting them is mandatory before installing; the top standoffs ship flat and are bent by hand along the center line.

Included: the WFP-75 with cast iron door and facade, classic moulded refractory brick panels, the outside air adapter and blocking plate, and the top and rear standoffs. You supply an insulated chimney from the makers in Table 3 (lengths, elbows where necessary, associated components) and the 6" anchor plate, sold separately.

  1. Find the standoffs and their screws in the firebox.
  2. Separate the 2 top standoffs, bend each by hand along its center line and install them on top.
  3. Separate the 2 rear standoffs and install them on the back.

Install the fireplace only as described in the manual, using only components from the chimney manufacturers listed in Table 3.
Lighten, locate & level

Remove the refractory panels and the facade to lighten and protect the unit; wear gloves. Set it on a level, straight surface where the chimney needs the fewest offsets, and check the floor against the weight.

• To make the unit lighter to carry, remove the refractory panels: a Torx (T-30) bit for the two screws holding the andiron, then the floor panel, the brackets and side panels, and the back panel. Gloves are strongly recommended.
  • Remove the facade during installation: open the blower door (held by a magnet), remove the two screws holding the facade frame, pivot it forward at the top, detach the 2 springs and lift it off clear of the door handle. The door is best left on.
  • Choose the spot with windows, doors, traffic, the hearth extension, mantel, optional hot-air ducts, outside air kit and chimney in mind. Ideally the vent misses trusses, beams, studs, water pipes and wiring.
  • Usually no extra floor support is needed. Check the weight, 575lb (261kg) including refractory panels, faceplate and packaging, and the floor construction against local code.
The fireplace must be installed on a level and straight (not uneven) surface. Not outdoors, not in an alcove, not in a mobile home (Canada) or manufactured home (USA); the fireplace and chimney must be in an enclosure up to the attic.
Hearth extension

Non-combustible floor protection at least 16" (406 mm) in front of the hearth and 8" (203 mm) on each side of the door opening; R 1.00 when the unit sits on the floor or is raised 4" or less. Cover the joint with bent, continuous sheet metal.
Frame the enclosure

Sides and back in 2" × 3" or heavier lumber; front studs and headers no deeper than the top standoffs; no combustible framing directly above the fireplace for 80" from its base. Keep insulation off the fireplace.

• Frame the sides and back with 2" × 3" (5 cm x 8 cm) or heavier lumber. Front studs and the headers on top must be no deeper than the top standoffs, which can sit flush with the fireplace or set back ½" to suit the finishing material.
  • Run vertical studs from floor to ceiling at the sides, set back from the front edge by the thickness of the facing so it finishes flush. Add headers only where needed to support the facing and mantel.
  • Nothing in the area directly above the fireplace: it must stay empty of combustible framing for 80" (2032mm) measured from the base.
  • Don't pack required air spaces with insulation. The fireplace must not touch insulation or loose fill; cover the insulation around it with drywall.
  • For a fresh-air or forced-air kit, leave room so flexible pipe stays out of the standoffs. Those framing layouts and corner framing are drawings in the manual.

Check the building code on finishing material inside the chase.
Facing & mantel

Non-combustible facing in front of the fireplace to the minimums on the facing drawing, with the faceplate still removable. A combustible shelf 6" deep goes at least 58" above the fireplace base; a non-combustible one at least 48".

• Materials directly in front of the fireplace must be non-combustible and meet the minimum dimensions on the facing drawing. Brick, stone or ceramic tile may project in front of and onto the decorative frame.
  • The faceplate overlaps the surrounding material and must stay removable after installation; with thicker material, use a faceplate gauge to position it. The facade can be set for facing material between 3/8in and 1in thick behind it, and a non-combustible shim can center it.
  • Combustible shelf: 6" (152 mm) deep at least 58" (1,47 m) from the fireplace base. For other depths, add 52" (1,32 m) to the depth. The optional heat shield lowers this (6" deep at 50").
  • Non-combustible shelf: at least 48" (1,22 m) from the base, whatever its depth. It gets hot; keep combustibles off it.
Install the chimney

Use a listed 6" chimney from Table 3, starting with a 6" anchor plate secured to the fireplace. Frame square holes with 2" (50 mm) clearance, fit firestops and an attic radiation shield, lock each length, then add the roof support, flashing, storm collar and cap.

1. Cut and frame the holes in ceilings, floors and roof, lined up with a plumb bob and sized to the chimney maker's instructions: square, with 2" (50 mm) minimum to combustibles. Don't fill that space with insulation or anything combustible.
  2. From below, install a firestop at each ceiling/floor the chimney passes through; at the attic, install an attic radiation shield from above.
  3. Secure the anchor plate to the fireplace, then install and lock each chimney length per the chimney maker.
  4. At the desired height, install the roof support. Fit the roof flashing (on a sloping roof, under the upper shingles and on top of the lower ones), seal it with roofing pitch and nail it with roofing nails.
  5. Tighten the storm collar over the flashing, seal it to the chimney with silicone caulking, and install the chimney cap. Don't seal the openings of a ventilated roof flashing.
  • If the anchor plate's male nozzle is longer than 2" (51 MM), cut it above the lifting hooks so the plate rests flat on the fireplace. If you cut only around the hooks, check that the flue damper mechanism works before closing the walls.
  • Mandatory components (Table 4, p. 50): a ventilated roof flashing with Olympia Chimney Ventis; Selkirk Ultra-Temp (UT), Super Pro (SPR), Super Vent (JSC), Hart & Cooley (TLC) and Sure-Temp (ST); M&G DuraVent Dura Tech and Dura Tech Canada DTC; and ICC Excel 2100. Security Chimney (ASHT+, S-2100+) requires an insulated attic radiation shield unless the chimney is enclosed at the attic level. American Metal (HS, HSS) can't be enclosed at the attic level.
  • Rafter protectors must be installed at the roof level if the chimney is enclosed at the attic level: 22 ga or more galvanized steel, at least the size on the diagram on p. 51.
  • Maintain the structural integrity of floors, walls and roof, and enclose chimney sections that pass through accessible spaces. The roof chase must be the same size as the flashing.
  • Masonry chimney: have it inspected by a qualified chimney sweep first. It must be clean and sound, built to code, keep 1" between the masonry and wood framing or loose insulation, and serve no other appliance. Reline it with a stainless liner the same diameter as the outlet, enter through a hole drilled at 45° or 30° with an insulated liner adapter (30° only in the USA), seal with high temperature refractory cement and run the liner at least 12" (30 cm) above the masonry. The manual also says the fireplace hasn't been tested to be installed inside a masonry chimney, and it isn't approved for a positive flue connection to the clay tile.
Height, offsets & roof exit

At least 15 ft (4.6 m) from the fireplace base to the cap, or 17 ft (5.2 m) with four elbows. Run 3 ft above the roof and 2 ft above anything within 10 ft; brace it if more than 5 ft above the roof. Every installation needs at least one support.

Vertical15 ft. (4.6 m)
Two elbows15 ft. (4.6 m)
Four elbows17 ft. (5.2 m)
  1. Install the first elbow, turned the required way, and secure it per the chimney maker (often three ½" (12 mm) metal screws).
  2. Add the chimney lengths for the offset, locked together. An offset of two or more lengths may need an offset or roof support halfway; through a wall, use the chimney maker's wall radiation shield.
  3. Turn vertical with another elbow, cut and frame the next hole, and fit a firestop from below.
  4. A support must be used on the first 15' section (4.6 m).
  • Avoid deviations where possible; each adds restriction and may cause draft problems. Starting with a 30° elbow is approved (45° in Canada only).
  • The fireplace should carry no more than 9 ft. (2.75 m) of 2" solid pack or 12 ft. (3.7 m) of 1" solid pack chimney.
  • Extend at least 3 ft. (92 cm) above the roof contact and 2 ft. (61 cm) higher than any wall, roof or building within 10 ft. (3.1 m). Use a roof brace above 5 ft. (1.5 m). A rain cap is required.
  • A 15 ft. system is the minimum and needs optimal operating conditions.
Note: for a good draft, p. 43 recommends 18" (457mm) from the top of the unit to the furthest offset; pp. 47 and 48 recommend 18 inches (457 mm) to the first offset.
Outside air (if required)

Some US jurisdictions require outdoor combustion air, and the manual strongly recommends it. Fit the 4" adaptor on the right side or underneath, the blocking plate on the air-control box, and 10 to 30 ft of 4" insulated flex with a P-trap to an outside wall termination.

1. Right side: cut the knock-out's micro-joints, then cut out the insulation and the inner knock-out. Underneath: cut only the knock-out. Remove only the knock-out you'll connect.
  2. Fit the included adaptor, line up its notch with the one on the fireplace and turn it clockwise.
  3. Open the blower control door (the lower cast iron panel of the facade) and install the blocking plate on the front opening of the air control box.
  4. Clamp the 4" insulated flexible pipe to the adaptor and to the outside wall termination. Tape the duct-to-adaptor joint with aluminum tape, then put back the insulation and tape the plastic wrap.
  5. Cut the wall hole 1/4" to 1/2" (6 mm to 13 mm) bigger than the insulated pipe and screw the termination to the wall, open side down.
  • Pipe at least 10 ft, at most 30 ft (9 m), with a P-trap, to avoid condensation and rust. It can run inside the chase but must keep clearances to combustibles.
  • Termination: not above 50% of the chimney's total height, not more than 10 ft. (3 m) above the fireplace base and not more than 3 ft. below it. Air must come from outside, never from the attic, basement or garage.
  • A mechanical damper to close the intake when the fireplace isn't in use is strongly recommended.
Hot-air kits (optional)

Gravity kits (traditional 94-99100, modern 94-99110) take 8" rigid 26 ga ducting from the top knock-outs; the forced-air kit 94-57110 fits either side. Never connect the hot-air ducts to a central heating system.

Gravity kits

  • Remove the knock-outs over the two 8" (20 cm) holes on top, then cut out the insulation and the inner knock-outs.
  • Both kits: 8" rigid, 26 ga galvanized steel duct (not included); no insulated flexible duct and no «T» fittings; at least 12" (305 mm) from an outlet frame to a combustible ceiling, side wall or mantel; a firestop radiation shield with 2" (50 mm) around the duct through a combustible wall or floor.
  • Traditional kit: at least 68" (1.7 m) from the fireplace base to the top of the outlets; at most 10' (3 m) of pipe including elbows and two elbows per duct; runs only vertical or horizontal, never downward; always install both grilles, flaps pointing down.

Forced-air kit 94-57110

Fits either side (the left performs better) and moves heat to a room up to 50 feet (15 m) away. Use HVAC insulated flexible pipe to ULC S110 and/or UL 181, Class 0 or Class 1, rated to 250°F, and follow the kit's own manual. Used with a gravity kit, it draws some air from the gravity ducting and reduces its efficiency.

Note: p. 27 says not to connect the fireplace to, or use it with, any air distribution ductwork; pp. 57 to 64 describe the optional gravity and forced-air distribution kits with ducting, and pp. 58 and 62 say not to connect those ducts to a central heating system.
Wire the blower & refit the facade

A qualified electrician connects the supply to the blower's terminal block: white to white, black to black, ground to the fireplace's metal frame. Refit the facade, then fit the wooden knob on the door handle before the first fire.

• The blower (7211-9412) sits under the firebox; to replace it, remove the faceplate, the air control panel and the air control housing.
  • Wiring should be done by a qualified electrician: connect the wires from the power outlet to the terminal block, white to white and black to black, with the ground (green or skinned wire) attached to the fireplace metal frame.
  • Where there's no local code, follow CSA C22.1 in Canada or ANSI NFPA 70 in the USA.
  • Refit the facade in reverse order of removal, positioned for 3/8in to 1in of facing material behind it.
  • Before the first fire, fit the wooden door knob to the handle with the shoulder screw and the 5/32 hex wrench provided.

panels.title: Smoke & low draft
items: Smoke into the room → low draft when the door is opened, or exhaust fans creating negative pressure (worse in airtight houses)
Cold backdraft with no fire → chimney shorter than the heated space, or running up the outside of the house
Slow kindling, smoke roll-out when loading → signs of bad venting system design
Exterior chimney in a cold climate → low draft, heavy creosoting, poor start-up, down-drafting or flow reversal

panels.title: Over-firing · too much draft
items: Fire you can't control, very high temperatures → too much air
Reddish glow on the unit or chimney parts → overheating
Heavy fuel use, lower heating capacity → excessive draft
Overheating → more than three manufactured logs, or large amounts of paper, cardboard or branches

panels.title: Weak or smoky fire
items: Flames fade away after turning the air down → air reduced too early in the cycle, or wood too wet
Dense load smoulders → air turned down too much
Little heat, more creosote, dirty glass → green or unseasoned wood
Inefficient burns, low heat output → low draft

panels.title: Glass & door seal
items: Whitish dusty film after a week → normal; wipe it off when cool
Light brown stains in the lower corners → smoky, low-temperature fires
Brown streaks from the glass edge → glass gasket worn
Paper slips out of the closed door → door gasket worn; replace it, or adjust the latch

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
The best-practice method is the top-down fire. It needs well-seasoned wood.

  1. Make sure the air control is open.
  2. Crisscross about 10 pieces of finely split, dry kindling (0.5 to 1 in), leaving air space between them.
  3. Put at least 5 sheets of newspaper on top. Rolled into a long cylinder and tied in 2 knots, they burn slowly and cleanly.
  4. Light the paper and leave the door open 1 inch for 5-10 minutes.
  5. Once there's a small coal bed, crisscross three or four medium split pieces (2-3 in) and close the door.
  6. When you have a good coal bed, you're ready for the main load.

The classic way: bunch up 5 to 10 sheets of newspaper, add about 10 pieces of very thin kindling (less than 1") and some larger kindling. Open the air control fully, light the paper, and close the door once the fire catches. Commercial fire starters work too; use gel starter only in a cold firebox.

No flammable liquids such as gasoline, naphtha, fuel oil, motor oil or aerosols. Don't leave while the door is open a crack; close and latch it once the fire catches.
Your first fires cure the paint. The smell isn't poisonous, but it's unpleasant and can set off smoke detectors, so open doors or windows. Start with one or two small fires, then bigger, hotter ones until the smell is gone. Before the very first fire, fit the wooden door knob with the shoulder screw and 5/32 hex wrench provided.

air.title: Using the air control
air.html:
The air control is below the ash shelf, on the right. Push the handle all the way left (High) to open it and burn faster, or all the way right (Low) to close it and burn slower. The fireplace runs at three settings: maximum, medium and low.

  • Open it fully to light a fire and for each new load. Keep it open until the firebox is full of flames, the wood is charred black and its edges glow red. Then turn it down.
  • In EPA certification tests, the air stayed open about 5 minutes after the door closed, was set halfway, and 5 minutes later was closed completely for low or left partly open for medium.
  • Less air spreads the wood's heat over a longer time, and the flames slow down. With dry wood they get smaller but stay bright and steady.
  • If the flames shrink until they disappear, you turned the air down too early, or the wood is too wet.
  • To open the door while the fire is flaming, open the air fully for a few minutes first, then unlatch the door and open it slowly.
Too much air can make the fire uncontrollable and overheat the fireplace and chimney, and can even cause a chimney fire. A reddish glow on the unit or chimney parts means it's overheating. Running with the air fully open for whole burn cycles also wears parts out.
The lowest burn setting is set at the factory. Altering it is against federal regulations.

reload.title: Reloading & burn cycles
reload.html:
Wood burns best in cycles: a new load is lit by hot coals and burns down to a bed of charcoal about the size it started on. Don't try to get steady heat by adding one log at a time. Heat rises after you load, then tapers off. That's normal.

  1. Reload once the room has cooled a little.
  2. Remove ash first, then rake the coals, which collect at the back, toward the door.
  3. Load at least 5 to 8 pieces, ends facing you (north-south), on and behind the coals and not too close to the glass.
  4. Close the door and open the air fully. Never leave the fireplace unattended while the load fires hot, and don't over-fire it. Then turn the air down.

Build for the weather

  • Mild days: small 3" to 4" pieces, crisscrossed, give four hours or more. Softer woods help you avoid overheating the house.
  • Long, gentle burns: softwood packed tightly, up to eight hours.
  • Cold weather: the biggest hardwood pieces at the back, the rest packed compactly, for the longest burn the fireplace can give.

Before you leave a fire to burn, make sure it's flaming brightly. Rated maximum burn time is 9 h, but yours depends on your wood, load, chimney draft and home. When you're home to tend it, a smaller fire is often the better choice.

wood.title: Choosing firewood
wood.html:
Burn only natural, seasoned firewood. Ready-to-burn wood has a moisture content between 15% and 20% by weight. Wet wood is behind most complaints: more creosote, little heat and a dirty glass door.

  • Length: the WFP-75 fits wood up to 20"; the recommended length is 16". Keep pieces within 1" of each other.
  • Size: split to a range of about 3" to 6" across. Even 3" logs should be split so they dry.
  • Drying: stack it in the open, in sun and wind. Pine, spruce and poplar can be ready after one summer; oak, maple and ash can take one or two years.
  • Is it dry? Look for cracked ends and wood that has turned grey or yellow. Dry pieces knock together with a hollow sound, feel light, and don't hiss in the fire. A wood moisture meter also works.

Manufactured logs of 100% wood residue are fine: start with one and never burn more than three at a time. Use only firelogs tested for fireplaces, none with chemical additives, and don't poke or stir them while they burn.

Never burn unseasoned (wet or green) wood, scrap or garbage, lawn clippings, plastic or rubber, pressure-treated wood, railroad ties, plywood or particleboard, construction debris, salt-water driftwood, paint or paint thinner, waste petroleum products, asphalt products, manure or animal remains, materials containing asbestos, or large amounts of paper, cardboard or branches. Burning these may release toxic fumes, or make the fireplace ineffective and cause smoke. Salt or chemicals can corrode the firebox and chimney. Intense firing of large amounts of paper, cardboard, branches or construction materials may overheat the fireplace and damage it, cause a home fire, or even start a chimney fire if there's creosote in the chimney. Fire starters made of paper, sawdust or wax are fine for lighting.

blower.title: Running the blower
blower.html:
A blower comes installed behind the faceplate, at the bottom of the fireplace. It moves air around the fireplace's air jacket to circulate warm air into the room. Used regularly, it can add a small efficiency gain, up to 2%, but it won't make an undersized fireplace heat a bigger space.

Its controls are behind the blower control door, the lower cast iron panel of the facade: a rocker switch for the mode and a speed knob (rheostat).

  • AUTO: set the switch to AUTO and choose a speed. The blower starts by itself once the fireplace is warm and shuts off when it's cold.
  • MAN: set the switch to MAN and choose a speed. The blower starts right away and runs until you turn the knob fully to the left or change the mode.
  • Off: turn the knob counter-clockwise until the blower stops.
Any blower wiring should be done by a qualified electrician.

ash.title: Emptying the ashes
ash.html:
Take ash out every two or three days when you're heating full time. Letting it build up gets in the way of managing the fire.

  • Best time: after an overnight fire, when the fireplace is fairly cool but the chimney still draws enough to pull ash dust into the fireplace instead of the room.
  • Put the ashes in a metal container with a tight lid and take it outside right away.
  • Set the closed container on a non-combustible floor or on the ground, well away from anything that can burn.
  • Ashes usually hold live charcoal that can stay hot for several days. If you bury or spread them, keep them in the closed container until every cinder is cold.
  • Don't put any other waste in that container.
Never store ashes indoors, in a non-metal container, or on a wooden deck.

Before reloading, take the ash out first, then rake the coals toward the front.

glass.title: Glass & door care
glass.html:
With dry wood and good habits, a whitish, dusty film forms inside the glass after a week or so. That's normal. Once the fireplace is cool, wipe it off with a damp cloth or paper towel, then dry it. Never clean the glass hot, and never use abrasives.

  • Light brown stains, often in the lower corners in spring and fall, mean the fire has been smoky. Use a cleaner made for wood-heater glass. In mild weather, letting the fire go out can work better than keeping it going.
  • Brown streaks from the edge of the glass mean it's time to replace the glass gasket (self-adhesive, from your retailer).
  • Aim for clear glass. Stains that keep coming back mean your wood or the way you run the fire needs to change.

The door seal

After a year or more, the door gasket hardens and can leak air. Close and latch the door on a strip of paper, all the way around. If the paper slips out easily anywhere, replace the gasket (kit 94-58106). A latch adjustment can also improve the seal.

Cracked or broken glass: don't use the fireplace, and don't slam or strike the door. Replace the glass only with the same 5 mm ceramic glass (kit 94-58100). Tempered or ordinary glass can't take the heat.

chimney.title: Creosote & chimney fires
chimney.html:
Wood smoke can condense in the chimney as creosote, a deposit that can catch fire. Smouldering, smoky fires build it up quickly; clean fires with mostly clear exhaust build it up slowly.

  • Check the chimney monthly while you're getting used to the fireplace, until you know how fast creosote forms.
  • Have it cleaned and inspected at least once a year, ideally at the end of each heating season. Damp summer air mixed with deposits can corrode the steel, and corrosion isn't covered by the warranty.
  • Don't let more than 1/8" (3 mm) of creosote build up. Chemical cleaners won't keep it clean.
  • A professional chimney sweep is recommended, especially for the first cleaning. The baffle and air tubes come out for sweeping. Never run the fireplace without the baffle.

If the chimney catches fire

  1. Close the fireplace door and the air control.
  2. Alert your family. Call the fire department if you need help.
  3. If you can, use a dry chemical fire extinguisher, baking soda or sand. Never water: it can cause a dangerous steam explosion.
  4. Check outside that sparks and embers aren't lighting the roof.
  5. Don't use the fireplace again until a qualified chimney sweep or a fire department inspector has checked the chimney and fireplace.

safety.title: Safety & over-firing
safety.html:
• The fireplace is hot while it's in use. Keep children, clothing and furniture away; you may need gloves to tend it.
  • Keep the door fully closed while it burns. Open the air control fully before you open the loading door.
  • Keep anything combustible at least 48" from the front of the fireplace opening, and don't store wood within its minimum clearances.
  • Don't raise the fire on grates or andirons, and don't block the air inlets or hot air vents.
  • Don't use it with cracked or broken glass, firebricks or baffles.
  • Don't over-fire the fireplace; over-firing can result in a safety hazard.
  • Put smoke and carbon monoxide (CO) detectors throughout the home, including bedrooms and hallways, and test them.

Signs of over-firing

A reddish glow on the unit or chimney parts. Over-firing can permanently damage the fireplace and chimney, can lead to a chimney fire, and isn't covered by the warranty.

The optional fire screen

Open-door use with a rigid fire screen is prohibited in the United States and in provinces with a particulate emissions limit. If a screen is used, secure it so sparks can't damage the floor, and never leave the fireplace unattended, so someone can respond if smoke spills into the room. The screen also raises the risk of carbon monoxide; a CO detector is highly recommended.

Note: p. 6 says to operate the fireplace only with the door fully closed; p. 17 says it was tested for open-door use with a fire screen, beside the prohibition above (pp. 17 and 65).

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
HearthStone's limited lifetime warranty covers the original buyer only (it isn't transferable), for normal residential use, on products bought after October 1st, 2011. Parts / labour:

Combustion chamber (welds only), castings, convector air-mate, ceramic glass (thermal breakage only)Lifetime / 4 years
Plating (defective manufacture)Lifetime / n/a
Stainless firebox parts, surrounds, heat shields, trims, C-Cast baffle, secondary air tubes5 years / 3 years
Carbon steel firebox parts, glass retainers, handle assembly3 years / 2 years
Blowers, heat sensors, switches, rheostat, wiring, controls2 years / 1 year
Paint (peeling), gaskets, insulation, firebrick, ceramic fibre blankets1 year / n/a

Lifetime parts can be replaced once. Glass, plating, baffle and air-tube claims need pictures.

Not covered

  • Misuse, improper installation, lack of maintenance, over-firing, transport damage, power failures, downdrafts or venting problems
  • Scratches, corrosion, distortion or discoloration
  • Damage from unauthorized or non-original parts

An authorized qualified technician must do the installation. To claim, contact your HearthStone dealer with the bill of sale, the model name and serial number from the nameplate on the back of the unit, the installation configuration and the defect. Get an authorization number before shipping anything back.

specOutput.title: Heat output & efficiency
specOutput.html:
Overall heat output rate14,200 BTU/h to 48,200 BTU/h (4.16 kW to 14.13 kW)
Maximum heat output (dry cordwood)80,000 BTU/h
Recommended heating area750 to 2,200 ft² (46 to 186 m²)
Average overall efficiency68% (HHV) · 73% (LHV)
Optimum efficiency (LHV)74%
Particulate emissions1.14 g/h (EPA / CSA B415.1-10)
Average CO53 g/h

Certified to the U.S. EPA 2020 particulate emissions standard using cord wood (CFR 40 part 60, subpart AAA; ASTM E3053-17). Efficiency is the weighted average across 3 burn rate categories, by CSA B415-10 methodology.

The 80,000 BTU/h maximum is based on a 15 to 20 lb/ft³ loading density; the tested values use the standard's 7 to 12 lb/ft³ load at 19% to 25% moisture. Heating area and burn time vary with the home, chimney draft, climate and fuel. The manufacturer-set minimum burn rate must not be altered.

Door · glassSingle, cast iron frame · 5 mm ceramic glass, 13.65" x 25.3"
Door gasket84 inches of 1 in. rope (kit 94-58106)

East-west: you see the sides of the logs through the door; north-south: you see the ends. The four secondary air tubes (5411-071 to 5411-074) and the baffle come out for chimney sweeping; the tubes can be replaced without removing the baffle board. Fuel moisture should be 15% to 20%.

EPA certification loads (p. 11)

The loads used for emissions certification, with air space left between the pieces:

  • High burn, air fully open: 6 small pieces (2" x 2") crisscrossed in 2 layers (3 at the bottom, 3 on top), 10 to 12 finely split kindling pieces over them and five knotted sheets of paper on top; paper lit with the door fully open until the 2 top layers burn, then closed. When the kindling and small pieces have almost burnt out, level the coal bed and load 5 logs: 2 small (about 3" x 3") in a reverse V at the bottom, a big piece (about 5" x 5") east-west at the back over the V, and 2 medium (about 4" x 4") in front, one over the other. Door open at 90° for 3 minutes or until the fire is fully established, then closed; air left fully open.
  • Medium and low: on a 2" coal bed that is dark red, 6 pieces: 2 small (about 2.5" x 2.5") in a reverse V at the bottom, 2 medium (about 4" x 4") east-west at the back over the V, one over the other, a big piece (about 5" x 5") east-west in front over the V and a last medium piece (about 4" x 4") over the big one. Door open at 90° for 3 minutes 30 seconds or until the fire is fully established, then closed. Primary air open about 5 minutes, then halfway; after another 5 minutes, closed completely for low or partly open for medium.

specChimney.title: Chimney
specChimney.html:
Flue outlet / chimney6 in (150 mm)
TypeCAN/ULC S629, UL 103 HT (2100 °F), listed models in Table 3 only
Minimum system height15 ft. (4.6 m) vertical or with two elbows · 17 ft. (5.2 m) with four
Above the roof3 ft. (92 cm) above roof contact · 2 ft. (61 cm) above anything within 10 ft. (3.1 m)
Clearance to combustibles2" (50 mm)
Length the fireplace may carry9 ft. (2.75 m) of 2" solid pack · 12 ft. (3.7 m) of 1" solid pack
  • Start with a 6" diameter anchor plate (sold separately) secured to the fireplace. Every installation needs at least one support; use a roof brace above 5 ft. (1.5 m). A rain cap is required.
  • A dedicated flue: don't connect to a chimney flue serving another appliance.
  • An interior chimney performs better. Exterior chimneys in very cold areas are prone to low draft, creosoting, poor start-up and flow reversal, especially with a basement installation.
  • Separate neighbouring chimney terminations by 16" (410 mm) horizontally and 18" (460 mm) vertically.
  • Listed chimneys: Selkirk, Security Chimney, M&G DuraVent, ICC, Metal Fab, American Metal and Olympia Chimney models, all 6" (15 cm) inner diameter.

specClear.title: Clearances to combustibles
specClear.html:
Determined by test to ULC-S610 (Canada) and UL 127 (USA). No part of the fireplace may be closer to combustibles than these minimums.

Enclosure · back0"
Enclosure · sides0"
Floor under the fireplace0"
Chimney2" (50 mm)
Ceiling, from the fireplace base80" (2,03 m)
Wall in front of the fireplace48" (122cm)

Three more clearances, measured from the door opening, are given as lettered dimensions on the clearance drawing; read them there. The space directly above the fireplace must stay empty of combustible framing for 80" from its base.

Non-combustible means made entirely of steel, iron, bricks, tiles, concrete, slate, glass or a combination; gypsum counts only if certified for 250°F or more. Not approved for alcove or mobile home installation.

specHearth.title: Hearth extension
specHearth.html:
The WFP-75 can sit directly on the floor or on a raised combustible or non-combustible base. For any installation, the non-combustible hearth extension must reach at least 16" (406 mm) in front of the hearth and 8" (203 mm) on each side of the door opening.

#1 Directly on the floorR 1.00 required
#2 Raised 4" or lessR 1.00 required
#3 Raised more than 4"Non-combustible, no R value
Joint protectionBent, continuous sheet metal (not included), 2" (51 mm); #3: 2" horizontally and 2" vertically at the upper and lower angle
  • Continuous non-combustible material with grouted joints: ceramic tile, cement board, brick, millboard or equivalent. Any tile needs a continuous non-combustible sheet beneath.
  • R values add: four inches of brick (0.8) plus 1 inch of Durock (0.52) gives 1.32, which meets 1.00. Material values are in Table 1.
  • The floor under the fireplace should match or exceed the height of the floor protection. No carpet under the floor protection.

One more hearth-extension dimension is shown only on the requirements drawing.

specShelf.title: Mantel & shelves
specShelf.html:
Heights are measured from the base of the fireplace.

Combustible shelf

6" (152 mm) deep58" (1,47 m)
8" (203 mm) deep60" (1,52 m)
10" (254 mm) deep62" (1,58 m)
12" (305 mm) deep64" (1,63 m)

For a depth not in the table, add 52" (1,32 m) to the shelf depth to find the safe height.

With the optional heat shield

6" (152 mm) deep50" (1,27 m)
8" (203 mm) deep52" (1,32 m)
10" (254 mm) deep54" (1,37 m)
12" (305 mm) deep56" (1,42 m)

Non-combustible shelf

At least 48" (1,22 m) from the base, whatever its depth. It will be hot; don't put combustible materials on it.

specFraming.title: Framing & facing
specFraming.html:
Sides and back2" × 3" (5 cm x 8 cm) or heavier lumber
Front studs & headersNo deeper than the top standoffs
StandoffsFlush with the fireplace or set back ½", to suit the finish
Directly above the fireplaceEmpty: no combustible framing for 80" (2032mm) from the base
Fireplace to faceplate3/8" gap minimum (built in)
Facing behind the facade3/8in (minimum) to 1in (maximum)
Weight575lb (261kg) incl. refractory panels, faceplate, packaging
  • Side studs run floor to ceiling, set back by the facing thickness so the facing sits flush. Headers only where needed to support the facing and mantel.
  • Don't pack air spaces with insulation; the fireplace must not touch insulation or loose fill. Cover insulation with drywall.
  • Materials directly in front of the fireplace must be non-combustible, to the minimums on the facing drawing; the faceplate must stay removable. Keeping the non-combustible material flush with the fireplace is recommended.
  • Flexible pipe in the framing enclosure must not run within the standoffs. Fresh-air, forced-air and corner framing are shown as drawings.

specAir.title: Outside air & blower
specAir.html:
Some US jurisdictions require outdoor combustion air; in Canada it isn't required if a CO detector/alarm is in the fireplace room. The manual strongly recommends an outside air intake, a mechanical damper to close it when the fireplace is off, and a CO detector in the room.

IncludedOne 4" adaptor, an air inlet block-off plate, four screws
Duct (not included)4" insulated flexible, ULC S110 and/or UL 181 Class 0 or 1, rated to 250 °F
Duct length10 ft minimum · 30 ft (9 m) maximum, with a P-trap
InletRight side (most common) or right side underneath
Wall terminationNo higher than 50% of the chimney's total height or 10 ft. (3 m) above the fireplace base; no more than 3 ft. below it
  • Air must come from outdoors, never the attic, basement or garage. Keep the termination clear of snow, extreme wind, car exhaust, gas meters and other vents; avoid a heavily windward wall.
  • Check the outdoor air duct for soot when the venting system is cleaned.

Blower: included, up to 176 CFM (7211-9412). Wiring by a qualified electrician: white to white, black to black, ground to the fireplace metal frame.

conflicts.issue: Open-door use with the fire screen: p. 6 says 'OPERATE ONLY WITH DOOR FULLY CLOSED'; p. 17 says the fireplace has been tested for use with an open door in conjunction with a fire screen (sold separately); a line on pp. 17 and 65 says that in the United States or in provinces with a particulate emissions limit (e.g. US EPA) the use of an open-door wood fireplace with a rigid fire screen is prohibited.

Ductwork: p. 27 says 'DO NOT CONNECT TO OR USE IN CONJUNCTION WITH ANY AIR DISTRIBUTION DUCTWORK', while Appendices 4-6 (pp. 57-64) give optional gravity (94-99100, 94-99110) and forced-air (94-57110) distribution kits with ducting, and pp. 58 and 62 say only not to connect the hot air ducts to a central heating system.

Offset recommendation: p. 43 recommends 18" (457mm) from the top of the unit to the 'furthest offset'; pp. 47 and 48 say 18 inches (457 mm) to the 'first offset'. p. 43 also limits a 45° starting elbow to Canada, which p. 47 doesn't (p. 48's masonry note gives 30° only in the USA).

review.notes: One 76-page installation & operation manual (6400-41420; the cover's revision date is cut off as 'R: 30/04/202'). The cover also prints 'FP15 Waterloo' above 'WFP-75 Model 8411'; that name appears nowhere else and isn't used in the guide. SCRAMBLED PAGES RE-CHECKED: pp. 3, 11, 17, 50, 51 and 65 (and the p. 8 labels) came through in a font shifted by 29 code points with invisible digits; they are now decoded in doc1.txt, numbers included, and every statement that depends on them was re-checked against the decoded text (the earlier hand-decoded caveat no longer applies). Confirmed as written: the air control (p. 11: below the ash shelf on the right; handle fully left = High/open, fully right = Low/closed); the prohibition on open-door use with a rigid fire screen in the United States and provinces with a particulate emissions limit (pp. 17, 65), now also stated plainly in the safety drawer, with the p. 6 / p. 17 conflict kept; the 5-to-8-piece north-south loads, the open-door rule while flaming and the blower modes (p. 17); the 'Overall Firebox Volume' 2.5 ft³ (0.071 m³) (p. 8). Changed: the air drawer now links p. 11 (was p. 19 with a note pointing to p. 11); the fire-screen sentence no longer ties the carbon monoxide risk to leaving it unattended (p. 17 gives smoke spillage as the reason, and CO risk with a CO-detector recommendation separately). Added: the certified air turn-down (air drawer) and the EPA certification loads, high and medium/low (p. 11, specFirebox); the EPA loading volume 1.69 ft³ (p. 8, specFirebox; its metric value is still partly shifted in the text, so it is left out); Table 4's mandatory components by chimney (p. 50) and the 22 ga galvanized-steel rafter protectors (p. 51) in step5. Residue still in the text: p. 11's medium-burn setting reads 'ó´ open' (one glyph undecoded), so the guide says only 'partly open' and points to p. 11; on p. 11 the degree sign after 90 (door open at 90°) is lost and inch marks show as ´; a few p. 50 cells remain shifted ('9HQWLV' = Ventis, '6ROLG 3DFN $6+7' = Solid Pack ASHT, 'sentilated' = Ventilated, '^` qriple wall : ep/epp' = AC Triple wall : HS/HSS) and were read against Table 3 and the reading-order extract; p. 8's volume values are still shifted in the layout text ('OKR ft EMKMTN m F', '1.69 ft EMKM48 m F') but read 2.5 ft (0.071 m ) in the reading-order extract; p. 17's blower letters 'E_F', '^rql', 'j^k' are (B), AUTO, MAN; the p. 3 residue is in table-of-contents lines only (2.4 EPA certification loading, 2.4.1-2.4.3 on p. 11). FIGURES NOT TRANSCRIBED: general, internal and faceplate dimensions (pp. 9-10, drawings only); the clearance letters on p. 29 (A 3" max, B 8" min, C 13" min, from the door opening) because the text doesn't say what each marks, so the catalog's 'side trim from door opening 8"; side wall from door opening 13"' can't be confirmed from the text (numbers agree, labels unverified); the hearth-extension B 41-1/2" on p. 34; framing E/F and C/D (pp. 36-37); duct framing J/M (p. 38); corner framing (p. 39); facing O/P/Q/R (p. 40); the rafter-protector dimensions (p. 51, diagram labels only). The safety rating label (p. 71) has no text, so no blower electrical rating or label data is in the guide. OTHER: p. 42 prints 'continuous temperatures below 18 C (0 F)' (minus sign missing); the guide says 'very cold areas' instead. p. 54 lists the outside-air adaptor as '4" (76mm)'; the guide uses 4", matching the 4" pipe elsewhere. Table 1 (p. 33) lists ceramic tile at k 12.5 and R 0.008 per inch, which don't agree; the table isn't transcribed. p. 2 points to the warranty section for registration instructions, but the warranty (p. 72) has none. p. 27 says the fireplace hasn't been tested to be installed inside a masonry chimney while pp. 48-49 give a relined masonry-chimney connection; both are shown in step5 as written. The general rule of 5 to 8 pieces per load in north-south orientation (p. 17) sits beside smaller crisscross and east-west fires (pp. 19-20) and the east-west EPA certification loads (p. 11); all are shown. The manual has no troubleshooting chart; the four fault panels are built from its fault descriptions on pp. 2, 14, 15, 19-21, 23, 42 and 54. All checkable catalog specs (heating area, 80,000 BTU/h, 68% HHV, 1.14 g/hr, EPA 2020, 9 h, 2.5 cu ft, 20 in logs, 6 in flue, blower included, 80" ceiling, 58" mantel) match the manual. Catalog features not in the manual: Matte Black / Brown Enamel finishes and the 'hand-chiseled' front.
